segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the third day there was a wedding in Cana of Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus too was invited to the wedding, along with his disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the wine ran out, the mother of Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “They have no wine.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And Jesus said to her,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Woman, what is this to me and to you? My hour has not yet come.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His mother said to the servants,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Do whatever he tells you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now six stone water jars were standing there, for the purification rites of the Jews, each holding two or three measures.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Fill the jars with water.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they filled them to the brim.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Now draw some out and take it to the master of the banquet.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they took it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When the master of the banquet tasted the water that had become wine—he did not know where it came from, though the servants who had drawn the water knew—the master of the banquet called the bridegroom

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Everyone serves the good wine first, and then the poorer wine once people are drunk. You have kept the good wine until now.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus did this, the first of his signs, in Cana of Galilee, and revealed his glory, and his disciples put their trust in him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After this he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and they stayed there a few days.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Passover of the Jews was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the temple he found those selling cattle, sheep, and doves, and the money changers sitting there.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Making a whip out of cords, he drove them all out of the temple, both the sheep and the cattle; he poured out the money changers’ coins and overturned their tables,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and to those selling the doves he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Take these away from here! Stop making my Father’s house a house of trade.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His disciples remembered that it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “Zeal for your house will consume me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So the Jews responded and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “What sign can you show us for doing these things?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Destroy this sanctuary, and in three days I will raise it.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Jews then said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It has taken forty-six years to build this sanctuary, and you are going to raise it in three days?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he was speaking about the sanctuary of his body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: While he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, during the festival, many put their trust in his name, seeing the signs he was doing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But Jesus, for his part, would not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and had no need for anyone to testify about a person, for he himself knew what was in a person.

notes.phrase: what is this to me and to you
notes.traditional: what have I to do with thee? / what does this have to do with me?
notes.note: The Greek is a set idiom, literally “What to me and to you?”, familiar from the Septuagint. It usually means “What business do we have with each other?” and can range from a hostile rebuff to a mild refusal to be drawn in. Some take it here as “What concern is that of ours?”, others as “Why do you involve me?” Either way Jesus distances himself from the request, and the next sentence gives his reason.

In Greek this was a normal and courteous way to address a woman, without the brusqueness “Woman” has in modern English. It is nevertheless an unusual way for a son to address his mother. Jesus uses it for her again from the cross (19:26).

notes.traditional: two or three firkins / twenty or thirty gallons
notes.note: The measure named here was a standard liquid unit of roughly ten gallons (about thirty-nine liters). Each jar therefore held some twenty to thirty gallons, and the six together well over a hundred. Stone vessels were favored for purification water because stone was held not to contract ritual impurity.

notes.traditional: governor of the feast / master of the feast
notes.note: The word is rare and denotes the person in charge of a dinner. It is not certain whether this was a head servant who managed the food and wine or a guest chosen to preside over the feast. His easy manner with the bridegroom in verse 10 may favor the second.

notes.traditional: when men have well drunk / when people have drunk freely
notes.note: The verb means to become drunk, and many versions soften it. The speaker is quoting a general rule of hospitality with some humor; the remark does not say that the guests at this wedding were drunk.

The verb covers both “believe” and “trust”. “Trust” is used here and in verse 23, where John has the construction “believe into” a person, so that the wordplay in verses 23–24 can be heard: many trusted in Jesus, but he did not entrust himself to them, using the same verb. In verse 22, where the object is the Scripture and Jesus’s word, the same verb is rendered “believed”.

notes.phrase: drove them all out of the temple, both the sheep and the cattle
notes.traditional: drove them all out of the temple, with the sheep and oxen
notes.note: The Greek can mean that Jesus drove out all the sellers together with their animals, or that “all” refers to the animals, “both the sheep and the cattle”. The grammar allows either, and scholars are divided. The rendering here follows the second reading while leaving the first possible.

notes.phrase: Zeal for your house will consume me.
notes.note: The quotation is from Psalm 69:9 (68:10 in the Greek numbering), a psalm of a righteous sufferer that early Christians often applied to Jesus. The psalm speaks of zeal that “has consumed” the speaker; John’s future tense, “will consume”, points ahead to Jesus’s death.

John often uses this term for the Jerusalem authorities and not for the Jewish people as a whole, and those who challenge Jesus’s right to act in the temple may well be its officials. Some versions therefore render “the Jewish leaders” here. The text does not identify them further, so the general term is kept. Jesus and his disciples were, of course, Jews themselves.

Greek has two words that most English versions both render “temple”. The word in verses 14–15 names the whole complex with its courts, where the traders were. The word here names the sanctuary building itself, the dwelling place of God, which suits its application to Jesus’s body in verse 21. Scholars differ on how strictly New Testament writers keep the two apart, and verse 20 is often cited as a looser use. “Raise” is the same verb used for Jesus’s resurrection in verse 22.

notes.phrase: It has taken forty-six years to build this sanctuary
notes.traditional: Forty and six years was this temple in building
notes.note: The Greek can mean that the building was completed over forty-six years or that it has been under construction for forty-six years so far. Herod the Great began rebuilding about 20–19 BC, and work on the complex continued until the 60s AD, so the second sense fits the history. Counting forty-six years from the start places this scene around AD 27–28.

candidates.reason: The register fixes ναός as “sanctuary” in contrast to ἱερόν, so ἱερόν needs a fixed rendering (“temple”) for that contrast to hold across the New Testament.
A key Johannine term that versions render variously as “sign”, “miracle” or “miraculous sign”; it should be uniform and distinct from δύναμις and τέρας.
The vocative γύναι recurs on Jesus’s lips (John 4:21, 19:26, 20:15; Matthew 15:28; Luke 13:12) and sounds rude in English though polite in Greek, so one policy is needed.
Used for raising buildings, rousing sleepers and resurrection; “raise”, “raise up” and “rise” should be chosen consistently so that links like John 2:19–22 survive.
Very frequent in John and Acts, with versions alternating between “testify”, “bear witness” and “give evidence”; it should match the rendering of μαρτυρία and μάρτυς.

warnings: Verse 24: πιστεύω is not rendered with a register form (believe / trust) and has no register-exception note.
